previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a male with relapsed multiple myeloma, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, type 2 diabetes, and chronic diastolic heart failure, was admitted after experiencing syncope during physical therapy at home. The episode was determined to be vasovagal, likely triggered by exertion and dehydration, with no evidence of cardiac arrhythmia, DVT, or infection. During admission, he experienced an acute flare of hemolytic anemia, managed by increasing prednisone from 7.5 to 10 mg daily, with stabilization of hemolysis markers. His kidney function showed transient worsening, attributed to pigment nephropathy from hemolysis, but improved with IV fluids. Diabetes management required insulin adjustments due to steroid-induced hyperglycemia, followed by a reduction after a hypoglycemic event. He was discharged home in stable condition on optimized medications, including increased folic acid and new vitamin B12 supplementation, with follow-up planned for hematology, cardiology, and primary care.

Brief Hospital Course:
Mr. ___ is a ___ man with multiple myeloma s/p

carfilzomib/revlimid, along with CKD Stage III, autoimmune 
hemolytic anemia, hypertension, Type II DM, and atrial flutter
with recent admission for syncope admitted from the ED with 
recurrent syncope.

# Recurrent Syncope: Recent admission for similar which was 
thought to be secondary to neurocardiogenic syncope. He had 
evaluate with TTE, bilateral ___, and ___ which were 
all unrevealing. At that time he was reportedly straining on 
toilet to have a bowel movement. During this current episode, he 
was reportedly sitting on the cough after walking, which seemed 
more concerning for primary cardiac issue. ___ were 
negative here. EKG was stable (RBBB, bifascicular block) and 
intervals otherwise reassuring. Pt never had any chest pain or 
dyspnea. Trop at baseline (0.11 recent baseline stable 
troponins). Tele without events. It was postulated that perhaps 
excessive beta blockade contributed, given HR noted during 
recent admit and on this admit to be in 50-60 range (SR) so his 
carvedilol was decreased to 6.25mg BID from 12.5mg BID. His 
amlodipine was increased from 5mg to 10mg as a result to 
maintain blood pressure control. He did not have any events on 
tele nor further episodes of syncope clinically. Cardiology 
evaluated him. They felt that he likely had neurocardiogenic 
syncope, agreed with lowering beta blocker dose. There was 
nothing to suggest a higher grade block. They noted that 
occasionally patients with neurocardiogenic syncope do have less 
symptomatic episodes when pacers are placed but at this time 
there was no clear indication for pacer and given overall 
clinical status and prognosis much preferred to hold off on 
pacing placer given not clear it would be of benefit. He will be 
discharged with a Zio patch (will have to walk over to 
cardiology clinic on discharge to have this placed, but 
appointment was made for him and he and his daughter were 
instructed on this). He will follow up with his cardiologist as 
an outpatient. At time of discharge he had no complaints and was 
ambulating around the floor all day.

# Chronic Hemolytic Anemia: Patient chronic anemia likely 
secondary to multiple myeloma, chemotherapy, and hemolytic 
anemia. H/H stable on admission. Recent admission prednisone was 
increased from 7.5mg daily to 10mg daily which he continued.

Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted after another fainting episode. We lowered 
your dose of carvedilol (a blood pressure medication) because 
that might have been keeping your heart rate too low and 
contributing to your symptoms. We monitored you here and you had 
no other problems. Our cardiologists evaluated you and felt 
there were no other undiscovered issues. 

It is important however you go home with a heart monitor. This 
is a patch that will just sit on your chest. You need to go over 
to the cardiology clinic immediately after you leave the floor 
here to get this patch applied. you must have this applied 
before you go home. The cardiology department is on the ___ 
floor of the ___. You can let them know you are 
there for the ""Zio-patch"" (that's the name of the monitoring 
patch) application and they'll help you out.

We recommend you have someone with you 24 hours a day in case 
there are any episodes of fainting, but we feel that on the 
lower dose of the carvedilol you have done well here under 
monitoring and you will continue to do well.

It is very important you continue your high pressure compression 
stockings at home to keep your legs from getting too swollen.

Because we decreased the carvedilol, we went up on your 
amlodipine to keep your blood pressure under control. You will 
take 6.25mg carvedilol twice a day and amlodipine 10mg daily.
